title: Evie White Started With a $50 Goal. Four Years Later, Her Longview Lemonade Stand Had Raised More Than $7,000
thumbnailMessage: A $50 goal became $7,000 for East Texas
summary: Longview’s Evie White turned a school fundraiser into an annual charity lemonade stand. By age 12, she had raised more than $7,000 over four years and selected Martin House Children’s Advocacy Center for her fifth campaign.
content:
A child’s first fundraising goal does not have to be large to change a community. In 2022, Longview student Evie White set out to raise $50 with a lemonade stand for Hiway 80 Women and Family Services Center. She collected about $1,800 instead—and kept going.

By the time Evie prepared her fifth annual stand in May 2026, the 12-year-old had raised more than $7,000 for East Texas organizations across the first four years, according to KLTV and Martin House Children’s Advocacy Center. She chose Martin House as the beneficiary of the fifth campaign, with 100% of the donations designated for the nonprofit’s work with children and families.

The result deserves recognition for what can be verified. Evie created a repeatable act of service, invited neighbors to participate and directed the money to established local organizations. RepWatchr has not found a published final total for the 2026 stand, so this article does not add that event to the more-than-$7,000 four-year figure or guess how much it collected.

The origin was simple. KLTV reported that Evie’s school participated in a 2022 fundraiser for Hiway 80. She decided to open a lemonade stand outside the Walmart on Gilmer Road in Longview, hoping to contribute $50. Community response multiplied that goal roughly 36 times. Instead of treating the surprise as a one-day success, she made the stand an annual project.

That persistence is the heart of the story. A first fundraiser can benefit from novelty. A fifth requires planning, supplies, adult help, public trust and a willingness to ask again. It also requires choosing a beneficiary and explaining why the cause matters. For 2026, Evie directed attention to Martin House Children’s Advocacy Center.

Martin House serves children in Gregg, Harrison, Marion and Upshur counties. Its multidisciplinary model brings together advocacy, forensic interviews, law enforcement, child-protection professionals, prosecutors, medical services and mental-health support after suspected abuse is reported. The center says it helped 1,026 children in 2025. That number belongs to the organization’s official reporting; it is not an estimate produced by RepWatchr.

A children’s advocacy center exists because forcing a child and family to navigate separate agencies alone can add confusion and trauma to an already difficult situation. Coordinated services aim to reduce repeated interviews, connect families with specialized help and support investigations without placing the burden on the child. The work is serious, confidential and often invisible to the wider community. A lemonade stand gives neighbors a safe, public way to support it.

Evie’s project also demonstrates a useful model for youth service. The product is familiar and affordable. The event has a clear beneficiary. The organizer states that all donations go to charity. The location is accessible and the appeal is local. Supporters can understand what they are joining without a complicated pitch.

Adults still have responsibilities whenever a child leads a public fundraiser. A parent or guardian should supervise money handling, location permission, food safety and transportation. Donors should be told whether they are giving directly to a nonprofit or through an individual fundraiser and should receive an official receipt when tax documentation matters. None of those safeguards diminishes a child’s leadership; they protect it.

The reporting around Evie’s stand reflects those good boundaries. Her mother, Sarah White, helped explain the history and the family’s commitment. Martin House publicly promoted the event. Local television identified the time, place and beneficiary. Those elements let neighbors distinguish an organized community fundraiser from an anonymous online request.

There is another lesson in the original $50 target. Small goals can make public service feel possible. A student who hears only about million-dollar campaigns may conclude that charity belongs to wealthy institutions. A pitcher, a card table and a willingness to talk to neighbors offer a different message: service can begin with what a family already has and grow because other people choose to join.

The more-than-$7,000 total is meaningful, but it is not the only measure. Each annual stand puts the selected organization’s name in front of shoppers who may not have known where to seek help or volunteer. It gives adults a chance to model generosity for their own children. It teaches the organizer about preparation, communication and accountability. Those effects cannot be converted responsibly into a dollar figure, but they are part of why a repeated local effort matters.

Recognition should stay proportionate and factual. Evie is not being credited with providing professional advocacy services or personally resolving abuse cases. Martin House’s trained staff and partner agencies do that work. Her exceptional contribution is building a dependable community channel that sends money and attention toward the professionals who help vulnerable children.

The community can honor the example without turning it into pressure on one child to fundraise forever. The strongest response is replication. A church youth group could choose an established pantry and publish a collection list. A school club could organize a supervised supply drive for a shelter. A neighborhood could support a volunteer fire department after confirming its official donation channel. The project should match the organizer’s age, capacity and safety needs.

It is equally important to verify beneficiaries. Donors can check a nonprofit’s official website, service area, contact information and public filings. They can ask how gifts are used and whether an event is authorized. For organizations serving children, public reporting should protect client identities while still explaining programs, governance and broad outcomes. Martin House provides public information about its counties, partners and services without exposing children.

East Texas hero stories do not always involve a dramatic rescue. Sometimes the exceptional act is returning to the same card table year after year, keeping the promise that the money belongs to someone else and giving a community an easy reason to help. The courage is quieter: naming a painful need, standing in public and trusting neighbors to care.

Evie White’s story began with a goal most families could imagine—$50. Four years and more than $7,000 later, the project had become an annual Longview tradition. The fifth stand’s selection of Martin House connected that tradition to children across four counties who need trained advocates at the hardest moments of their lives.

The final 2026 amount should be published by the organizer or beneficiary when available, and any future total should be dated so it is not confused with the four-year figure. Until then, the verified accomplishment stands on its own: a Longview student turned one school assignment into years of generous, accountable community action.
